text_fidelity_a:
RUB1ZR0 Red Green Dot Reflex Sight Scope Adjustable Reticle with 20mm Rail Mount This scope came in an excellent package with tools and batteries (1 installed and 1 extra) and instructions on how to set it up. There are 3 brightness settings for both red and green lasers and choice of red or green lasers on top of the scope and in back of the lens. The G and R letters are the Off positions. Keeping the Off position set when not using it will save battery life. On the top back of the scope are 4 reticle settings by sliding the switch back and forth to choose the one you want to use. All the settings are a little firm to move but stay in place afterwards.

First thing I did was mount the scope and secure to a picatinny rail. After mounting, I used the adjustment screw on top of the scope for elevating the up or down setting. I also used the adjustment screw setting on the left side of scope to zero in the laser. You can do this for up to 100 yards away but make sure you’re on a flat secure surface. I only needed to do small adjustments. This Rub1zro is in my opinion a quality item and a good value for the price.
text_fidelity_b: RUB1ZR0 Red Green Dot Reflex Sight Scope Adjustable Reticle with 20mm Rail Mount

text_fidelity_a: FAMELEY Camping Stove/Backpacking Stove, Portable Stainless Steel Wood Burning Stove with Nylon Carry Bag for Outdoor Hiking,Traveling and Picnic First off let me say that for the money this is a decent wood burning stove. I have used it now about 4 times and in a pinch, I am glad I have it. Positives: it works, its durable, the casing does not get super hot so you won't burn your self if you have to move it,  and it packs down small. Areas for improvement: First, I think the air flow holes/vents need to be a bit larger. After burning some wood some of the ash began to clog up the holes which did not allow good air flow. Second, (probably my biggest concern) it is difficult to keep adding fuel to this stove. Once you put the pot on top of it...it only leaves a small gap so in order to keep adding fuel you have to remove the pot for a second to add fuel so when you take the pot off the direct heat it starts to cool down. It would be nice if it had a cut out on one of the sides to be able to add wood without removing the pot. It took about 20 minutes to get a nice boil for two cups of water. So if you have time to just kick back not a big worry but if you are on the trail and want to stop for a quick lunch probably not the stove for you. Overall, I am glad I have it but probably will use it for emergencies and not so much on the trail.
text_fidelity_b: FAMELEY Camping Stove/Backpacking Stove, Portable Stainless Steel Wood Burning Stove with Nylon Carry Bag for Outdoor Hiking,Traveling and Picnic

Danielson unisex-adult Anchor Pulley Gray One Size I installed one of these on each end of an Old Town Pack canoe.

For installation, I cut a small board to act as platform for the pulley that I mounted onto the canoe. Then attached the pulley onto the board. This was necessary so the pulley would hang out over the end of the canoe enough.

The installation was easy enough with the screws received with the pulleys. But, I purchased separately 1/4" brass screws with nuts as I don't think the small screws would hold for long term. Not really a criticism.

But, the pulley has a restraining device that works very well, if your anchor rope is at least 1/2" diameter. Smaller cord I am using (purchased from Amazon with a Yak Gear Nylon Rope) will not restrain when you release the cord trying to hold the anchor in place. Must instead use cleats to hold the rope, which is difficult when you pull up the anchor and it is dangling off the end of the canoe. I have a 5# mushroom anchor on either end and that is significant weight to tie off.

Not sure this is the final solution with these pulleys and the nylon rope and I may have to go back to using larger diameter rope. Really did not want to do this as this would put more rope cluttering up the canoe when I fish.

These are well made metal anchors. Just not sure about for canoe/yak applications unless you can deal with the additional mass of rope in the boat.
text_fidelity_b: Danielson unisex-adult Anchor Pulley Gray One Size

text_fidelity_a:
Saris Solo Single Bike Rack First non-roof or truck box rail mounted rack purchased. Was in need for an inexpensive rack to put on the old Chevy Prism(Toyota Corolla) to carry a single bicycle. When unboxing I had some serious doubts. Chunk of light weight plastic. Nothing substantial like the Thules & Gorge Racks owned. Gave it a try. After a few uses I'm happy.

Set up is pretty much idiot proof. I leave the lower straps adjusted to fit the vehicle length. Loosening or tightening the top straps to remove or attach the rack. Take less than a minute. Rack when not used sits inside the trunk. Compact size takes little space in the Chevy's small trunk. No loose parts to lose.

My private driveway and mile of "gravel" township road traveled to reach pavement are by any standards poor. Pot holes, dips, bumps, washouts and rumble strip sections make for a harsh ride. Concern for the bike's paint job & my trunk door resulted in couple additions to the rack. 2 sections of foam pipe insulation to protect the top tube where the bike attaches to the rack and a velcro strap to keep the front wheel from flopping around. Saris incorporates a strap to keep the crankarms from rotating and pedal bumping your vehicle. Rack so far has functioned as advertised. Securely attached bike to the rack. Rack securely attached to your vehicle on smooth paved highways to bumpy gravel roads.

Only couple issue so far. 1st is more due to the road conditions & type of (trunk mount system). Dust & mud kicked up by the vehicle's backwash ends up on the bike more so than a roof system. 2nd is bike security. The rack to be removed at least on my car requires opening the trunk ~1" to release the lower mounting clips. Bending the clip with a small pry bar or just cutting the poly straps would allow for quick thief of the rack. Locking the bike to the rack requires some form of aftermarket cable & lock system. But then the thief could just take the rack with bike attached. Will need to think of some form of locking system to reduce the chance of this situation from happening.
text_fidelity_b: Saris Solo Single Bike Rack

text_fidelity_a:
Henderson Women's Thermoprene 3mm Front Zip Shorty Springsuit, Black/Lavender, 8 I got my first Henderson Zip Shorty a couple years ago for snorkelling on the Big Island. It was SUPERB! There is simply no easier style for getting into and out of a wetsuit on hot, steamy days or peeling them off when they're all wet. It's super easy to step into one of the legs and then zip the shorty up as high as you like. There is JUST the right amount of give in the armpits so you can swim but not fill the suit with water. It's a brilliant design, actually. The 3mm thickness was absolutely perfect for swimming in HI's water - where temps averaged 71-74F for us.

After each use, I'd faithfully soak, then rinse the suit out with special neoprene detergent, then roll it in a beach towel and hang it up to dry in the shower stall. It would be clean, fresh, dry and ready to use within a couple hours - even in a humid place.

I wore a long-sleeved rashguard under mine for extra sun protection, but otherwise, was totally warm enough with great flexibility for swimming in this garment. At the end of our 3-mo stay in HI, I donated my Henderson - and the dive shop nearly cried for joy!

Flash forward 2 years, and I bought the identical suit for snorkelling on Kauai! If I was psychic, I never would've donated the last one, and now I'm going to be an optimist and keep this one!

CAVEAT!!! Be sure to soak, WASH, rinse your suit out before you try it on - seriously! I just wore mine for 10-15 min day one and woke up later that night with a shorty-shaped RASH on my skin. I only read about neoprene reactions after that - and immediately washed my new shorty. Err on the cautious side, cuz that was the one and only time I got a rash, and you can avoid that if you just wash it first.

Of course, if you don't want to remove the tags, you could also try your wetsuit on with a "skin" underneath - but be sure to wash that garment then to avoid any neoprene reaction.
text_fidelity_b: Henderson Women's Thermoprene 3mm Front Zip Shorty Springsuit, Black/Lavender, 8

The only thing I don't really like is that it doesn't have any "machinery" for the clip-on seats with some back support. I've learned that wearing a small backpack helps with back support, but as is, the kayak is not "tall" enough for you to comfortably sit and lean into.

The menu interface is simple enough to use with easy to follow instructions in the manual. I had no problem getting it set up. I was able to capture several of the critters that visit our backyard pond, both on photo and video. I set it for the highest resolution possible but the images are not very good. I included a 100% crop of one of the javelina (collared peccary) photos along with the fullsize version for review. Along with a night photo and a night video (of our fox!)

I dont expect very high quality from night shots so these are what I expected for that. The videos are good and, again, the night ones are good. We finally got a decent video of our resident fox, too! (video included, if it uploads okay!)

Overall I'd say if you're looking for some quick images to capture wildlife this will do the trick. It's simple to use and produces "good enough" photos and videos. But if you want clearer, sharper images, you will be disappointed with this camera.

Oh, the largest memory card (SD) it will take is 32MB. We get a lot of critters at the pond - this was still taking photos/videos after 10 days out there even at the highest resoluation settings for both video and photo.

Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit We do a lot of camping and living outdoors, and something we enjoy is easy to make food when we are outdoors. We look for ways to keep the cooler, extra stoves, skillets, dutch ovens and cast iron at home. I think we found our answer in Mountain House freeze dried entrees.

We purchased the Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit. In it we chose the Beef Stroganoff and took it to a scout meeting to try. During the scout meeting we talked about light weight backpacking as well as food options for emergency food at home.

After we boiled two cups of water we poured it into the pouch and zip locked it for 8 minutes. The contents where stirred and then served to many hungry scouts at the meeting. Every scout got a sample to try and a lot of them were hesitant. The overall surprise on their faces was priceless. They liked it and said it tasted great.

They wanted a pouch of the Beef Stroganoff for themselves. The scouts were surprised how easy the meal was to make and how simple the cleanup is. We did also like the zip lock feature not only for the re-hydrating process but also to keep the uneaten food for later if needed. They were also coming up with ways to reuse the pouch for other needs in the forest or on the trail to keep from throwing the empty pouch away.

Most of the scouts have never re-hydrated food or eaten MREs before. They were impressed with the ease of cooking and how lightweight it is to add to your day pack or back pack.

For camping, outings or emergency preparedness I would recommend Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit to have on hand. For one it has a long shelf life, for two you won’t starve as the contents of each pouch will satisfy a hungry kid or adult. A very tasty meal…especially in the middle of the forest!

Our only complaint (and the reason we deducted a star) is not all the water absorbed into the food, so it was very runny. The pack instructed to use 2 cups of water and I feel that was too much.
text_fidelity_b: Mountain House Just in Case 72 Hour Kit

text_fidelity_a:
5.11 Tactical Bail Out Bag Molle Ammo Magazine Carrier Pack for Responders , Style 56026 5.11 is a well-known and highly regarded supplier of tactical equipment. This is a well-constructed bag made of a double-stitched tough nylon material that uses heavy duty zippers and large Velcro fasteners to keep everything locked down. It will hold six 30 rd mags of .223 ammo (or several other ammo combinations) securely and within easy reach. I put a piece of old towel between each pair of mags to help minimize any noises while moving around.

Behind the mag pockets is a deep compartment that can hold an effective combination of equipment. If you're like me, you'll want to also isolate any equipment in that main compartment to avoid shifting and noise generation. Each side of the bag has an additional zippered compartment that can hold pistol mags, a flashlight or other tools. The padded and adjustable shoulder strap can be configured to hang around your neck and allow the bag to be centered on your lower belly and there is a Velcro belt loop on the inside of the bag so that you can anchor it to a 2" belt. I prefer to have the bag centered so that I can get to what I need quickly with either hand.

This 5.11 Tactical Bail Out Bag is a well-made and practically designed grab bag that can be filled with critical supplies should you need to get out of your home in a hurry. The main problem I see is that the very bottom of the main compartment seems to be constructed of a thinner material. Unfortunately, because this large main compartment will hold a lot of stuff, the combined weight and/or sharp edges of whatever is being carried is likely to wear through that area first. This area needs to be reinforced by sewing in extra fabric or by the insertion of a fitted piece of foam. Either quick fix should add extra durability to this weak point. I'm very surprised that 5.11 didn't pay more attention to this part of the bag. Perhaps in the near future their bags will come out with some type of reinforced bottom.
text_fidelity_b: 5.11 Tactical Bail Out Bag Molle Ammo Magazine Carrier Pack for Responders , Style 56026

text_fidelity_a:
Neso Tents Beach Tent with Sand Anchor, Portable Canopy Sunshade - 7' x 7' - Patented Reinforced Corners Ack, my husband and I just took our new Neso Tent down to the beach today ... and lasted about 45 minutes under scanty shade with not enough head room. We SO wanted to love this shelter, as it has a brilliant concept: idiot-proof setup and very transportable kit, with the fabric and two collapsible poles all in one tidy storage bag.

In looking at the videos and even pictures of this particular model of Neso Tent, it appears that WIND is a HUGE factor in one's satisfaction with the overall experience. Alas, we sat on a hot, sunny, windless beach by the lake, so we found the fatal flaw real fast: without wind to literally LIFT the fabric up in the air, it sits flat and low at back. We could barely fit our slim selves in two beach chairs under that fabric. With the poles lifting up the front, the back of the fabric slopes down so low that our heads literally poked into the fabric overhead like two beach balls. Duh.

Not only that, but even on a windless beach, you're gonna need some serious LEAD weight to hold the 4 corner ropes in place. We hunted around our beach and found 3- to 5-lb river rocks. Once you raise the poles under the fabric, it literally lifts the corner ropes up in the air unless they are weighted down GOOD. To show a few handfuls of sand tossed into each pouch doing the job is simply misleading, unless that sand is made from lead shot.

On top of which, in order to face the view - i.e., the lake - we had the sun slanting in from the side. As soon as we set the tent up, that meant that one of us sat with legs in the burning SUN the whole time. Yes, even with our chairs scooched back so far that our dorky heads poked into the fabric, the total shaded area of this fabric is simply too small, measuring about 6' square. We probably could've re-positioned the tent with our backs facing the sun, but then we would've been staring at two bikini-clad gals lying on their beach towel 5 feet away - kind of in-your-face? Nope. It was no go.

Frustrated, we packed the tent up and will be sending it back. I think the perfect beach shelter should actually be more like a camping tent, with full coverage overhead and multiple, collapsible poles strung through the structure. Ideally, this tent would have net sides to let the breeze come through (and probably filtered sun). Most of the tents I see here are simply too HOT and airless, cuz they're made more for all-weather camping. Or they're shelters like 8' tall and 12' wide, which - if the two of us parked that on our little lakeside beach - would encourage others to beat us with their rubbah slippahs.

Best way to enjoy the beach is to slather up in sunscreen, leave all the food, drink, books and stuff at home. Go with a towel and get in the water. Period.
text_fidelity_b: Neso Tents Beach Tent with Sand Anchor, Portable Canopy Sunshade - 7' x 7' - Patented Reinforced Corners

text_fidelity_a:
Rubbermaid Victory Jug, 2 Gallon, Modern Red FG153004MODRD We debated whether to buy this water jug or another, more sturdy jug by another manufacturer for more than twice the money. We decided to buy the other jug when we found the Rubbermaid on sale at a local store for less than 1/3rd the cost of the more sturdy jug. For the difference in price we thought we'd give the Rubbermaid a try to see how it would perform.

The lower spigot on the Rubbermaid is solid. No leaks and easy to use. The upper vent spigot is a little bit of a weak point. It works absolutely fine, just remember to always close it so it doesn't get broken or let hot air cycle into the cold interior of the jug.

Although not an "extreme" cooler jug, once filled with ice and water we had cold water well into the second day in the desert. The cooler was kept in the shade the entire time.

If you need a rough and tumble water jug, look elsewhere. If you need something that will sit on a picnic table for a day or two, this will work fine.
text_fidelity_b: Rubbermaid Victory Jug, 2 Gallon, Modern Red FG153004MODRD

text_fidelity_a:
Klymit Maxfield Backpacking Tent, Lightweight 2-Person Tent for Camping and Hiking Honestly this tent is great, especially at the sale price it periodically goes down to. It is literally lighter than my previous 1-person tent. The stakes it comes with are great which is rare, plenty of guy-lines already attached and coiled up at the tie-off points, no issues with ventilation or heat retention in the 3-seasons it is designed for. The rainfly, footprint, and base of the tent all clip together quite nicely and have adjustment sliders to keep them correctly tensioned. The single piece pole assembly is a little counter-intuitive, but it works great once you orient it.

HOWEVER: get the footprint for it.

I bring a scrap of tarp to throw under the footprints of all my tents anyways, because a sharp, half buried rock can always ruin things, but you don't need to. A significant amount of the versatility and convenience goes away without the footprint that is designed for it, like the ability to throw the footprint and rainfly together as an emergency shelter in a few moments, or use it in an ultralight configuration to save even more weight.
The only potential concern i have is that with how light this material is, I don't know what long term durability will be. It is VERY light material, and that usually trades out durability. Time will tell.
text_fidelity_b: Klymit Maxfield Backpacking Tent, Lightweight 2-Person Tent for Camping and Hiking

text_fidelity_a:
ALPS Mountaineering Tri-Leg Stool I like to hike, and meditate during my hike. Sometimes for extended periods of an hour or more. While there are sometimes benches or natural features of the landscape that work well for meditation, this is not always (or usually) the case. I bought this hiking stool, to see if it would work well for this purpose.

I can happily report that for me, it works PERFECTLY for this task! I do not need back support while meditating, and for my height (5'6") I am able to sit on this stool with my legs at a comfortable roughly horizontal position to the ground. For a taller person, you may have to cross your legs, and they will not be horizontal to the ground, but that may be OK for you.

The stool is lightweight (I have no problem carrying it around for several hours, and there's a handy strap so it can just be slung over my shoulder) and presents no issues as a hiking companion. I did a nice sit with it yesterday for an hour in the woods at a park here in Baltimore. Lovely!

While there are a couple of inflatable zafu-style meditation pillows available on Amazon, I actually think for my purposes, this stool is superior. It will continue to come with me on hikes I intend to meditate during. I got mine on Prime Day, and I think it came to roughly five dollars with a ten dollar discount. Even if it had been about fifteen bucks at the standard price, it would be an excellent value.
text_fidelity_b: ALPS Mountaineering Tri-Leg Stool

Coleman Camping Tent with Instant Setup, 4/6/8/10 Person Weatherproof Tent with Integrated Rainfly, Double-Thick Fabric, and Included Carry Bag, Sets Up in 60 Seconds I've had this for about 3 years now, and I really do enjoy it. This is the go-to car-camping brought-way-too-much-stuff tent for fine weather. My husband likes it because he doesn't have to crawl to get around in it. I love that I can get it up in a few minutes without help. It's roomy and comfortable, but there are caveats.

-This is a single-layer tent without a rain fly. You can't leave the windows open in damp weather, and you WILL get tons of condensation in wet or cool conditions. It hasn't leaked badly in the rain for me, except when the rain has blown through the top vents. Keep your things away from the sides if you don't want them wet.

-I absolutely don't trust this thing in stormy or windy weather. It's just way too high profile for that sort of thing.

-It's bulky. I can easily fit it into the bag it came in (without needing to open the expander), but it's still large and heavy for a tent of these dimensions.

In short, this is a nice tent for a weekend with a fine weather forecast. It's not a tent for when you're going to be hours from civilization for longer than you can trust a weather forecast. Get yourself something low-slung with a fly that goes to the ground for that kind of camping.

text_fidelity_a:
Cold Steel Pocket Bushman Just received this knife as a gift from Cold Steel Special Projects. I had ordered a discontinued Spectre ($400 knife for $100)directly from them but the final shipment didn't meet their standards. As an apology, they shipped me a Pocket Bushman. By the way, the Special Projects web site offers great deals on discontinued models (like the Rajah) for significant savings.
My first thought was "what's a Pocket Bushman?". That was quickly answered when I slid it out of the box. Very strong and utilitarian looking tool. But I still didn't really get it until it opened with a bang and locked up fast and tight. It's just over 10 inches long when opened with a 4 inch razor sharp (and I mean RAZOR SHARP)blade. I told my wife that it was sharp enough to shave with and then immediately cut myself by trying to close it without looking at the instructions. You'd think that I would be smarter than that at my age. One quick swipe and the tip of my index finger started leaking blood through a cut that you could barely see. Blood everywhere.

This is a big cumbersome tool that will handle any task you set it to. Cold Steel's motto seems to be "If it's worth doing, it's worth overdoing". If you have to pull it out in a defensive situation, your opponent is going to think twice about engaging you. The intimidation factor is impressive--and it inspires confidence in your hand. Take my word for it. It's not for amateurs and will do accidental damage quickly.
"If you find yourself in a fair fight, your tactics suck!"
text_fidelity_b: Cold Steel Pocket Bushman

It is a short, stubby, relatively heavy .45 acp semi auto pistol available in stainless steel.. While it won't win any beauty contests, it has a presence all its own and the intimidation factor it provides is awesome. It's the kind of weapon that when you run out of ammo you can hit your opponent in the face with it for the game winner.

This ZT 0456 has that kind of look to it. It has some (short and stubby) curves but the overall construction is what draws attention to itself. Yes, it is a bit on the (slightly) heavy side, but this knife wasn't designed to be slim and beautiful. It is designed to work, and work hard, taking on any task from cutting to prying that you come up against. How many knives do you have in your collection that can be carried in your pocket, can dispatch any simple cutting jobs with aplomb, and then allow you to pry open a door with it. Most EDC blades don't have the spine for it, much less the overall design and build that would allow even attempting that task.

As I have aged I have learned that a knife should be much more than just a cutting tool. None of my automatic knives can even approach the type of hard work that this Zero Tolerance knife can conquer. The blade is sharp but heavy, the locking mechanism is tight and solid, and the flipper works like butter. People notice it when I pull it from my pocket, not just because it's a knife but because of the attractive and unique design. Everyone wants to know what it is, how much it costs, and where can they "legally" get one. This is one of those places.

text_fidelity_a:
2 in 1 LED Headlamp Flashlight Combo, 150 Lumens, Ultralight Waterproof, 1.2oz,Compact, Full-metal body, for Running, Camping Hiking, Cycling, Kids,ONLY 1 AA battery req & Incl 1 Energizer AA.COLORDAY 5/26/22 Still my everyday carry light, still going strong. Still waterproof, still gets dropped occasionally and comes back for more. I've worn most of the anodizing off down to bare aluminum. It's not a flamethrower, but for 99% of my needs, 80 lumens for 5+ hours is way more useful than 1500 lumens for 10 minutes. This light just keeps on trucking.

2/20/18 Still going strong, my everyday carry light.

1/16/17 Bumped up to 5 stars, the replacement light has been perfect. I lubed the tailcap threads and O-ring with petroleum jelly as soon as I received it, this might help.

11/15/16 Colorful Days replaced the light even though it was beyond the warranty period, quite nice of them. Will see how long this one lasts. Back up to three stars for now.

11/7/16 Downgraded to one star. Light flickers and is quite dim. Reacts to tailcap being unscrewed or tightened, and sometimes only works after loosening the tailcap slightly. Poor connection between tailcap and body of the light - useless.

So far so good. Solid little light and significantly less expensive than the Fenix and 4Sevens and Zebralight flashlights I keep losing. Headband is comfortable. The little case is nice enough but no one is ever going to keep the light in it - 5x more bulky than the light and headband alone.

With the cost reduction vs the brands mentioned above, some compromises are made. While it runs on rechargeable batteries, it's not really happy doing so. Much dimmer. I don't think the regulation circuitry likes the lower voltage much vs primaries much. The claim of 150 lumens is a joke, WAG compared to other lights I have, I would put this at ~80 lumens.

Can't comment on durability or waterproofness yet.

So far, while I'm happy with the light for the money, there's a reason I bought higher end lights. If my better lights don't turn up soon I'll just buy another one and this light will eventually get relegated to backup duty.
text_fidelity_b: 2 in 1 LED Headlamp Flashlight Combo, 150 Lumens, Ultralight Waterproof, 1.2oz,Compact, Full-metal body, for Running, Camping Hiking, Cycling, Kids,ONLY 1 AA battery req & Incl 1 Energizer AA.COLORDAY

Put one end of the tubing (connected to inlet side) up over the barrel into the water, & pushed the 1/4" outlet tubing (side with arrow pointing out) into the reducer which was screwed onto a 40 ft garden hose which was stretched out uphill.  I wasn't sure this small pump would move water uphill from a 55 gal barrel for that distance, but after several minutes, water started trickling out of the garden hose onto one of the bushes I wanted watered.  The trickle was just right to have it soak in as I did other chores then came back to move the hose to the next bush. text_fidelity_a:
Slime 10056W Bike Tube Puncture Repair Sealant, Prevent and Repair, Suitable for All Bicycles, Non-Toxic, Eco-Friendly, 16oz Bottle Used it, Loved it ... on the single wheel on my electric unicycle (EUC).
Where the rubber meets the road, it seems, doesn't get enough love here. So I thought I'd start a thread to share opinions about tire pressure, maintenance, etc. (starting with some of my opinions).

I find tire pressure to be one of the most important components of handling and ride, and I'm a bit obsessive about it on my EUC's (probably carrying over from motorcycles and bikes). There are three things that make tire pressure a challenge with EUC's:

EUC's only have one tire, low pressure has a direct impact on ride, and tire failures are unforgiving
EUC's have unique bent valve stems that make it hard to find inner-tubes, and a pain to fill (you just don't want to do it)
EUC tire pressure is a bother to check compared to any other vehicle, because the valve stems are hidden in the EUC cavity, and difficult to attach to a pump
... and there are probably other things. The net result is that you want to maintain the tire, fill to pressure and forget it.

To that end, I've Slimed (https://www.amazon.com/Slime-10056-Tube-Sealant-oz/dp/B003V9XYNW/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1487706156&sr=8-2&keywords=slime+bicycle) both my V8 and Zero. I used about 1/3rd of the bottle on each one. There is no effect whatsoever on the feel of the wheel, and I think it provides a certain security. In Chicago, I can take my bike into any number of convenient shops to buy and install a new inner-tube; but the same shops would just draw a blank with an EUC, and the inner-tubes are hard to find. Best to maintain what you have.

I like to keep my tire pressure up at 3 bar (~44 psi). The sidewalls of my V8 and Zero tires both recommend 40-65psi pressure, and the V8 comes from the factory at 2.8 bar (~40psi). So for me 3 bar seems the right pressure, and both wheels feel good at that pressure. It's a real bother to fit a pressure gauge on the valve stem because they are bent against the wheel. I almost never get a seal on my gauge without several tries.

So instead, I pumped the wheels up with my Lezyne pump (https://www.amazon.com/Lezyne-Steel-Floor-Drive-Black/dp/B005UND3CY/ref=sr_1_3?ie=UTF8&qid=1487706504&sr=8-3&keywords=lezyne+pump) -- I recommend Lesyzne as the absolute best bike pump on the market -- and then put a Gozens 44psi cap (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01HRIKIY0/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o04_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) on the wheel. That way, I can easily check the pressure at the start of each ride. You do need to buy the Gozens at a particular pressure (BTW, they have bluetooth systems, which I think are a bit of overkill) but you get 4 of the basic caps for $9, so NBD.
text_fidelity_b: Slime 10056W Bike Tube Puncture Repair Sealant, Prevent and Repair, Suitable for All Bicycles, Non-Toxic, Eco-Friendly, 16oz Bottle

Advanced Elements Summer Shower We've evolved as backcountry campers from sponge baths to the solar shower. Taking a bath in the backcountry is a daily requirement for us. At the end of a long day nothing feels better than washing off the dust and the sweat. In the past we'd heat 2 quarts of water to boiling on the stove then dump it in 2.5 gallons of cold water in a collapsible bucket. Then we'd sponge ourselves clean. This camp shower feels downright decadent compared to our previous habit.

For spring/summer camping it heats up to a nice warm temp in about an hour in the sun when the outside temp is in the low 70's. I wash first and use less than a gallon to get wet, wash, and rinse. Then my wife uses the rest of the water for the same, including washing/rinsing her shoulder length hair. We have two of them and occasionally she uses some of the water from the second one to finish rinsing her hair, but not always.

The shower head is a two-handed operation to pull it open for full flow or push it closed to stop the flow. We haven't had any problem with it at all. Great product.

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit Charge 3 Fitness Activity Tracker I'm a Fitbit lover. I track everything with it; steps, heart rate, activity, sleep, food, BMI, body fat. All these metrics warm my geeky little heart and help me achieve my health goals. I own a Flex, an Alta HR, and the Aria 2 scale and have adored all of them. Because I love them so much, I gave my husband a Charge 3 for his birthday. I'm sorry to say, this Fitbit product is a total dud. The tracker will not sync with Fitbit's app. It worked for about 1 month then just stopped syncing with the app. We've tried every flavor of delete-reinstall-reset possible, all to no avail. There are hundreds, maybe thousands, of people who have this same issue, who have reported it to Fitbit, and the response is unfortunately not in keeping with the company's usual excellent customer service. All they will offer people is another Charge 3. You can't even swap the tracker for a less expense, older model that works with their app. Without the app, without the ability to track and review a history, the Charge 3 is little better than the freebie plastic pedometers your employer's health insurance plan hands out at their annual Open Enrollment fair. What's more than a little irksome is that Fitbit seems unwilling to admit there's a major software problem here. Seems obvious when one reads the Help forums. Why not 'fess up and tell us an estimate of when we can expect a software update? I don't get it. People will likely be patient and wait for the update if they know one is in the works. What is to be gained by pretending nothing is wrong? A lot of very unhappy customers, that's what.

Long story short: Don't buy this tracker. Get a different one. Maybe even one not made by Fitbit (sorry, Fitbit!)
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Charge 3 Fitness Activity Tracker

text_fidelity_a:
Coleman Evanston Tent Updated Sept 2022. Purchased in 2018:

We use this tent three to five times per year depending on how many people are going. This is a great tent! The instructions on whether or not to use the black poles or the grey poles for the main tent could be clearer, but we wrote that on the bag after setting it up incorrectly twice.

I would not classify this as a three season tent, unless you live in a warmer climate. I live in central Texas, so this will work for me almost year round.

The good :
-very spacious, Large framed door on hinges.
-Good Head room.
-Lots of mesh on roof and two sides.
-Rain fly has excellent coverage over all openings but still allows adequate ventilation.
-Bath-tub floor comes up really high.
-Appears to be good reinforcement at stress points.

The bad :
- Really needs two people to set up (but I suppose if you are buying a tent this large you will have help).
- Stakes. As with any tent now a days, you probably won't be using the stakes that are included.

Buying experience - The tent arrived well before the stated delivery date, and the packaging was in excellent condition.

We now have six tents and three of those are Coleman Tents of various sizes. I have been generally pleased with the products overall, but I do not subject them to harsher environments as I would my Marmot or Eureka.

Warranty - Coleman stepped up and replaced this tent way past the warranty period. We got a rip in one of the sleeves for the main pole. Even though it still sets up OK, we felt it best not to use the tent in case a storm with gusty wing came up (because of the tear).

Hope this helps somebody.
text_fidelity_b: Coleman Evanston Tent

All Pro Weight Adjustable Ankle Weights, 10-lb pair (up to 5-lbs per ankle) These are comfortable -- very well padded -- and the weight is easy to adjust. However, the product has a few issues:

A) Worn over bare skin they tend to slide up and down a lot when doing more explosive movements, e.g. plyometrics or even something lighter like hamstring curls. I don't think this has much of an effect on the quality of exercise but it's annoying and slightly disconcerting.

B) Due to (A) I often try to really lock them down, and that's very tricky given the velcro fastening system. It would be very nice to have, in addition to the velcro, some way to tighten things further via a strap closure or something. (Or fix (A) using some different material.)

C) Probably also related to (A) -- they don't breathe very well. After a longer/harder session they can be a bit wet.

None of these are really a big deal, thus I only removed a single star. I think this is a quality product. And I think all of these defects could probably be fixed the same way, by reconsidering the material on the inside of the strap. Anyway, despite these minor flaws I'm happy with the purchase, and am already looking at buying a pair of the company's 10-lb weights to add to the mix.

text_fidelity_a:
KUBEY KU085 Tactical Folding Knife G10 Handle Stainless Steel Blade Bearing Flipper Hunting Pocket Camping Survival Outdoor Knife (#KU087) Nice knife, especially at this price point. BUT, there are some issues. To me it appeared that this this knife is inferred as being spring assisted. It is most definitely not spring assisted as all other knives are determined to be. The thumb hole is difficult for me to use in one smooth motion. I thought that surely the flipper would be spring assisted, but no. It takes it to half open and no more. You need to use a wrist flip or two hands to finish the opening. That would not be much of a problem, but that makes it illegal to carry here in central Ohio. Sad.

One last thing. This blade is nowhere near 4 inches. It is measured at 3.5 inches. How does Kubey justify these irregularities? Perhaps this is just something being lost in translation.

This knife is super sharp. Locks up like a vault. No wobbles anywhere. It handles well. And it is beautiful. It is definitely worth the money as long as you know up front what you are buying. The build quality is there. The cosmetics are there. It doesn't need this type of advertising to sell. Thus the four stars. I would buy again and I will probably buy from Kubey again.

UPDATE 78/1/17:

The screws holding the clip have become loose. I am in the process of buying a torx bit set so I can tighten them. I wish that this clip could be switched for tip up carry, but the clip orientation cannot be changed.

I have recently discovered that this knife's mode of opening does not make it illegal to carry in Ohio since it requires manually beginning the opening sequence by putting pressure on the blade. Ohio laws are very ambiguous as to what is or is not legal to carry. Happy camper here.
text_fidelity_b: KUBEY KU085 Tactical Folding Knife G10 Handle Stainless Steel Blade Bearing Flipper Hunting Pocket Camping Survival Outdoor Knife (#KU087)

text_fidelity_a: Wahoo TICKR Heart Rate Monitor, Bluetooth/ANT+ I bought this to replace a dying Garmin HRM I had.  Instantly, out of the box, you can tell the product design is better by the battery cover.  My garmin had 4 eye-glass screws that were easy to strip or gouge, while the Wahoo has a large sealed plastic cap (much less likely to break).  While cycling, I've almost never had any slippage or inaccurate readings, so I can't complain there.  While running though, the band's enclosure system is more difficult to synch tight and keep properly when you're running and sweating heavily.  It's a detriment of soft straps, but my old Garmin had pads that 'stuck' more to you.  All in all though, I'm super pleased; my work-around is just to make it really tight and then it'll loosen a bit as I run.  Data quality is very high (have compared to other HRM simultaneously)

M MAXIMUMCATCH Maxcatch 3-12wt Medium-Fast Action Premier Fly Fishing Rod-IM8 Carbon Blank for High Performance,with AA Cork Grip Hard Chromed Guides and Cordura Tube You see all of these reviews and they all start to sound the same, so I'll tell you where I'm coming from, my thoughts on the rod, and give my verdict.
I love fishing. There's nothing I'd rather do on the whole world. Nothing. You know what I mean... Lol! I've been fishing for decades, but have only been fly fishing for 3 years or so. I have several spinning rods in the $100-$200 range, and they are amazing. Unfortunately a $200 fly rod isn't the same as a $200 spinning rod. You can easily spend $3000 on a high end fly rod!

Well, I don't want to. I don't think it's necessary. But I've been fishing long enough that I can feel a great rod when I handle one. That's good, because I've seen lots of very expensive rods that were trash, and a few hidden gems that punched WAY above their weight. The Maxcatch Premiere line is one of those hidden gems. I picked this 3WT up just to check out, and after I effortlessly my fly 55' and landed it precisely where I wanted it. Over and over again. I mean it is so accurate that it's almost boring lol! And it's a $55 rod!

The blank is very sensitive, very light, very well finished and attractive, and the cork and dark chromed accents are beautiful. I'm surprised at how nice the cork is at this price point!

So I fish. A lot. I used to sell fishing equipment for a living, and I've handle a lot of gear. Is this Maxcatch a Loop or high end Sage? No. But it's also not $400-$900. However, I'd put this up against ANY Reddington, Fenwick, or lower end Sage any day and put money on the Maxcatch.

Get this rod. You'll be glad you did. You'll catch a ton of fish if you do your part, because this is a magnificent tool at an amazing price!

EDIT: I caught that monster 'Bow on the 4wt. Great fight! The rod was bent in half for 5 minutes, and held up great. And I felt every run, head shake, and dive. Great rods!
text_fidelity_b: M MAXIMUMCATCH Maxcatch 3-12wt Medium-Fast Action Premier Fly Fishing Rod-IM8 Carbon Blank for High Performance,with AA Cork Grip Hard Chromed Guides and Cordura Tube

WASING Outdoor Inflatable Lounger Nylon Fabric Beach Lounger Convenient Compression Air Bag Hangout Bean Bag Portable Dream Chair WS-InCOUCH-Blue I originally watched a viral video on facebook and saw that this type of lounger was available. I was curious about it. When this arrived in the mail, my husband immediately set it up and had me sit down in it. Instead of shaking it out (like you do with a garbage bag) he put it in front of a box fan and let it air up very quickly. Then you twist up the end and buckle it. It's extremely easy to use and light weight. It feels like a big balloon, but the material is a lot thicker.

When you sit on it, it feels like laying on a boat. It's soft, the air holds you up so you feel like you are floating. If you lay in the middle, go to reach for something, it will tilt back and fourth and feel like you are swaying on a boat in the water. My kids tried sitting on it and ended up sliding down inside it, so it's not really meant for little guys unless they sit on it like a chair or with someone. The more people on it however means the air escapes faster. If the air starts to escape after a while (an hour with one adult and two kids on it) then it is easy to fix that problem. Simply unbuckle the end, twist it a little tighter and re-buckle it. Then it's back to being nice and tight. When you are done it's easy to fold back down and put away.

This is such a neat idea for taking with you outdoors especially. It's rather long, my husband is around 6 1/2 feet tall and he can stretch out nicely on it. The material will make you feel sweaty after long periods in it, so just be aware when you are choosing how to sit on it or what to wear when you do. It's a nice luxury to take with you anywhere. Plus you don't need a pump to fill up the lounger.
